note.text: Read the whole passage before answering. Separate directly stated facts, reasons, proposals and information that remains unknown. An inference needs an identifiable clue and must not turn a fictional case into a universal claim. Notice who speaks and whether a statement is an opinion, a plan or an observed result. The passage is original classroom fiction, not a report about a real named organisation.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to distinguish a proposed response to an employment obstacle from a guaranteed result. Builds on: context clues, sentence structure and editing. Leads to: formal speech and evaluating proposals.

sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original passage: An imaginary youth group finds that some members hear about vacancies after the closing date. It proposes a noticeboard where volunteers copy opportunities and record sources and deadlines. Another member requests help describing existing skills. The group agrees that information and application practice may address particular obstacles but do not create every missing job. The pilot has not begun, so no later employment total is supplied.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Locate the relevant sentence, state your answer and identify its support. Check whether a question asks what happened, why, or what cannot be concluded. Do not add a result or private detail that the passage does not provide.
